reference.title: 'Returning' a question
reference.text: When you're having a conversation, you often 'return' questions, that is ask somebody the same question that they asked you. You can do this by: 1) saying And you? or What about you? 2) repeating the question, but stressing you, e.g. A: Where are you from? B: I'm from Rome. Where are YOU from?

tasks.instruction: Have a conversation. Ask and answer the questions in Getting to know you. After you answer a question, 'return' it

exercises.situation: You are a new classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate): Kasia, from Poznań, in Poland. Invent the rest of your life (home, family, job, free time) and keep it consistent. You and the student have the questionnaire 'Getting to know you': 1 Where are you from? 2 Where were you born? 3 Where do you live? 4 Do you live in a house or a flat? 5 Do you have any brothers and sisters? 6 Do you have any pets? 7 What do you do? 8 What time do you get up during the week? 9 Where do you usually have lunch? 10 What time do you usually go to bed? 11 Where did you study English before? 12 Can you speak any other languages? Which? 13 What kind of music do you listen to? 14 What TV programmes or series do you watch? 15 Do you do any sport or exercise? What? 16 What kind of books or magazines do you read? 17 How often do you go to the cinema? 18 What did you do last weekend? Take turns: ask the student questions from the list, and answer the student's questions. After you answer, often 'return' the question (And you? / What about you? / Where are YOU from?). When the student answers your question, wait: they should return it to you with And you? / What about you? — if they forget, give them a moment, then gently remind them once. Keep your answers short (1–2 sentences).

exercises.opener: Hi! I'm Kasia. Where are you from?
criteria: asks at least 5 questions from the questionnaire with correct word order
answers the partner's questions in full, natural sentences

uses the right verb in the questions (live, have, do, get up, go, speak, listen to, watch, read)

reference.title: QuASI
reference.text: Question word – Auxiliary – Subject – Infinitive. In the present and past simple we add do / does / did.
If there's a preposition, we often put it at the end of the question: Who do you live with?

reference.right: What time do you get up?
reference.why: Present simple questions need do / does.
With be the verb goes before the subject.

reference.wrong: What did you did last night?
reference.right: What did you do last night?
reference.why: After did the verb is in the infinitive.

tasks.instruction: Ask the first question. If the answer is Yes, ask the second question

exercises.situation: You are a friendly classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). The student asks you questions from this list. First they ask a Yes/No question; if you answer Yes, they must ask the follow-up question. PRESENT: Do you drink a lot of tea or coffee? → How many cups do you drink a day? / Do you go to a gym? → What gym do you go to? / Do you sleep well? → How many hours do you sleep? / Do you play games on your phone? → What games do you play? / Do you like watching sport on TV? → What sports do you like watching? PAST: Did you go to bed late last night? → What time did you go to bed? / Did you cook lunch or dinner yesterday? → What did you cook? / Did you go for a walk at the weekend? → Where did you go? / Did you see a good film last week? → What film did you see? / Did you buy any clothes last month? → What did you buy? Invent a consistent person. Answer Yes to most questions but No to one or two, so the student has to move on to the next question. Answer briefly and naturally (e.g. 'Yes, I drink a lot of coffee.' 'Three or four.'). If the student makes a word-order mistake, ask them to repeat the question correctly. Do not ask the student questions yourself except, occasionally, 'And you?'.
exercises.goal: Ask your classmate Do you…? and Did you…? questions.
exercises.opener: Hi! OK, I'm ready. Ask me your questions.
criteria: asks at least 6 of the Yes/No questions (Do you…? / Did you…?) with correct word order
after a Yes answer, asks the matching follow-up question with the right auxiliary (do you / did you)
uses both present (do) and past (did) questions
after a No answer, moves on to the next question instead of asking the follow-up

tasks.instruction: Communication: Alphabet quiz. Ask and answer the questions
tasks.note: SB 3e + Communication 1A (A p.102, B p.108): ученик — A, ИИ — B

exercises.situation: Alphabet quiz with an English student (pre-intermediate). The student is Student A, you are Student B. Take turns, starting with the student: the student asks their question 1, you answer; then you ask your question 1, the student answers; then the student's question 2, and so on. The student's questions (card A, with the answers): 1 Which country's security service is called the FBI? (the USA) 2 What do you use a USB cable for? (connecting something to a computer) 3 What can you do at a B&B? (stay the night and have breakfast) 4 Which famous writer has the initials JK? (J.K. Rowling) 5 What kind of person is a VIP? (a very important person) 6 What can you get from an ATM? (money / cash) 7 Which country's national radio and TV is called the BBC? (the UK / Britain). Answer them as a student would, mostly correctly, saying the letters clearly. Your questions (card B, with the answers — do not reveal the answers before the student tries): 1 What kind of machine is a BMW? (a car) 2 What does a DJ do? (plays music in a club) 3 Which country's national airline is called KLM? (Holland / the Netherlands) 4 What's the difference between a.m. and p.m.? (morning and afternoon) 5 What do people who work in IT do? (they work with computers, software, etc.) 6 How many states are there in the USA? (50) 7 In the UK do people have ID cards, passports, or both? (only passports). Say whether each answer is right; if it's wrong, give the right answer. Keep count of the student's correct answers and tell them the score at the end.
